newsitem.title: UK: Now Labour promises to let Britons decide on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Now Labour promises to let Britons decide on EMU.

text.p: The opposition Labour party, in a major policy decision, said on Sunday that if it won power it would hold a referendum before taking Britain into the European Union's planned single currency.

The announcement means all Britain's main parties will fight the coming general election committed to a popular poll on economic and monetary union (EMU). Prime Minister John Major's Conservative party promised in April to hold a plebiscite.
Labour sees the advantages of a single currency but, like the Conservatives, insists that the economic conditions must be right and says it will keep its options open.
Until now Labour has said it would seek consent for signing up for EMU, due to be launched in January 1999, either through a referendum or a general election.

But Gordon Brown, the party's economics spokesman, said it was now clear that crucial aspects of EMU would not be settled in time for Labour to make up its mind before the election, which must be held by May 22.

"We will not know all the details before the general election, and that's precisely why it's logical to say that if a decision is made during the course of the next parliament, the British people should have the right to decide in the way I'm suggesting -- through a referendum," he told BBC television.

With surveys showing voters largely hostile to the notion of scrapping the pound, Labour officials were concerned that the party's commanding poll lead could be eroded if it chose to fight the election on an overtly pro-European platform.
An NOP opinion poll in The Sunday Times gave Labour, in opposition since 1979, a lead of 20 percentage points over the Conservatives, up from 14 points a month ago.
The decision should enable Labour's leading spokesmen to close ranks, in the same way as Major's ministers did after the cabinet agreed in April to promise a referendum.

Strains have been evident between Brown, the leadership's leading pro-European, and foreign affairs spokesman Robin Cook, who in recent speeches has been pointing up the difficulties Britain would face in joining the first wave of EMU in 1999.
It will also make it harder for the Conservatives to prey on voters' worries about losing sovereignty by portraying Labour as determined at all costs to scrap the pound.

As a result, Major could come under pressure from "Euro-sceptic" Conservatives opposed to closer integration to rule out EMU during the next five-year parliament as a means of re-establishing a clear difference from Labour.

Brown denied that the positions of the two main parties was identical on Europe or that Labour was striking an increasingly Euro-sceptical tone. He said Labour was pro-European while the Conservatives presented themselves as an anti-European party.
"We support and see substantial benefits in the single currency, but we've always said the decision has got to be made in the national economic interest at the time," he said.
Sir James Goldsmith, who has founded the Referendum party to demand a plebiscite on Britain's role in Europe, remained disctnictly unimpressed with either Major or Blair.

Goldsmith spent as much as 500,000 pounds ($800,000) placing advertisements in Britain's Sunday newspapers calling Major "impotent" and Blair "dumb" in the face of what he sees as a fundamental transfer of power from London to Brussels. ($1=.6005 Pound)
